title: Video-Language Models: Temporal Tokens and Grounding

questions.question: Why is a video not adequately represented as an unordered stack of still images?
options: A video model must predict image pixels before it can answer questions.
Video frames do not contain spatial information about objects.
Temporal order and event timing determine what actions happened and when.
Every frame has a different vocabulary that a text encoder cannot read.
questions.explanation: Video meaning depends on event order and timing: the same still frames can describe different actions depending on which came first. An unordered image set loses before/after relations and cannot answer when an event occurred.

questions.question: What does Qwen2.5-VL's TMRoPE provide that a simple frame-index embedding does not?
options: Only the order of frames, without any row or column information.
Actual timestamps for each visual token, along with spatial coordinates.
A class label for every sampled frame.
A single learned position for the entire video clip.
questions.explanation: TMRoPE associates each patch with temporal, height, and width coordinates, using actual time rather than only frame index. When FPS varies, frame indices do not preserve the same elapsed-time spacing.

questions.question: A 5-minute clip is sampled at 1 FPS with 576 tokens per frame. How many visual tokens does it contain before compression?
options: 2,880 tokens, treating five minutes as five sampled frames.
300 tokens, from one token per second.
576 tokens, because one frame represents the whole clip.
172,800 tokens, from 300 seconds*1 frame/second*576.
questions.explanation: Five minutes=5×60=300 seconds; 1 FPS gives 300 frames, and 300×576=172,800 tokens before compression. The 2,880 option counts only five frames, while 576 counts a single frame.

questions.question: What sampling behavior distinguishes dynamic-FPS from uniform frame sampling?
options: Sample every frame at the source video's full FPS.
Allocate more frames to high-motion segments and fewer to static segments.
Choose equally spaced frames regardless of motion in the clip.
Keep only frames at detected shot boundaries and discard the rest.
questions.explanation: Dynamic-FPS allocates more samples to high-motion seconds and fewer to static ones, guided by motion intensity and a frame budget. Uniform sampling spaces frames evenly, which can miss brief action peaks between samples.

questions.question: A downstream event detector needs precise start and end times for a jump. Which output format is easiest to consume reliably?
options: Structured JSON with event name, start time, and end time fields.
A class label for the whole video with no timestamps.
An image caption with no event interval or coordinates.
Free text such as 'the jump happens near the middle of the clip.'
questions.explanation: Structured JSON exposes event, start, and end fields for direct downstream parsing; an interval such as start=4.1,end=4.3 is machine-actionable. “Near the middle” lacks a precise interval and requires ambiguous natural-language interpretation.

questions.question: A long clip keeps the sampled frame sequence but needs fewer tokens per frame. Which approach sacrifices some spatial detail to reduce context cost?
options: Remove temporal positions and keep all original patch tokens.
Pool each frame's patch grid before passing frames to the LLM.
Run a separate text encoder on each frame without pooling.
Use full-resolution patches for every frame at 30 FPS.
questions.explanation: Pooling reduces the patch grid within each sampled frame, lowering spatial tokens while retaining a coarser visual representation. Removing temporal positions or using full-resolution high-FPS frames does not reduce the per-frame spatial token cost.
